title: Norway have a secret weapon and two underrated stars, it's not just Erling Haaland and Martin Odegaard | talkSPORT
text:
The Bodo/Glimt star narrowly missed out on Norway's squad for the tournament after being called up for the March friendlies.

But having spent time with Stale Solbakken's team, and playing alongside a number of the key men domestically, Bjortuft knows exactly what they are all about.

The English focus will undoubtedly be on Premier League superstars Erling Haaland and Martin Odegaard as Thomas Tuchel's men try to progress through their quarter-final in Miami on Saturday - live on talkSPORT.

But Bjortuft believes Norway's overall togetherness is what stands in England's way.

When asked about the Norwegian perspective on England, the 27-year-old centre-back said: "We think that England is a better team, in a way.

"I think individually, they are pretty strong. But I think the collectiveness in Norway is much, much better than England.

"That's said from the outside, of course. I don't know what's going on inside.

"England have a lot of star players. We also have that. But I think we work better in a group, watching from outside.

"So I think that's where our hope is coming from. We know that the team is going to beat England, not [just] Haaland or Odegaard."

Norway have already made history by reaching the World Cup quarter-finals for the first time ever, sparking parties in the streets of Oslo and Viking rows across North America.

Bjortuft admitted the dark horses were initially just 'happy to qualify' for the tournament, but now there is a genuine feeling they can achieve something truly special.

And from his experience with Norway in the months leading up to the World Cup, there was already a feel-good factor inside the camp.

"It was a really good experience," Bjortuft said. "The lads were top.

"Everyone was really welcoming and fun to be around. I think that's a really good thing for Norway, because everyone is having fun together.

"Everyone is being together and playing cards, playing golf, as you've seen, in the States. I think that's the biggest X-factor of Norway: the team and the collectiveness they have.

"Everyone is enjoying spending time together. That's a good thing when you're at the World Cup and on a camp for two months, almost. That's the biggest part, I think."

The Norwegian football revolution has actually been years in the making with Bjortuft's club: Bodo/Glimt.

Football fans will be well aware of their fairytale in Europe, reaching the Europa League semi-finals in the 2024/25 season before qualifying for the Champions League knockout stages the following campaign.

Bjortuft was an important part of the team that stunned Manchester City, Atletico Madrid and Inter Milan along the way.

So was Patrick Berg - the grandson of iconic Norway legend Harald Berg - and the midfielder has caught the eye at the World Cup.

"[Berg] is much more important than people from the outside think," Bjortuft said.

"They may be looking at him as a good player from a small club, but he has huge respect in the national team and, of course, here also.

"He's a big player for us. But he's a leader, a really good leader.He leads, whether it's Haaland or me. It doesn't matter who he leads, because he's a really good leader outside of football.

"I think people respect him and his opinions of football. He's a really clever football head.

"I think he's influential in the national team. For me, he's maybe one of the best Norway players in this World Cup, which is pretty fun for us to see.

"It doesn't matter to him if it's the quarter-final in the World Cup or if it's Lillestrom here in Norway.

"He plays his style with the same ease of mind, which is extremely impressive for us."

Norway also have serious strength in depth on the bench in Andreas Schjelderup.

The 21-year-old Benfica forward has three assists at the World Cup despite only starting one match.

"Every time he [Schjelderup] has come in, he's made a difference," Bjortuft said. "He's a tough player to face, to say the least.

"He's really clever when he challenges you and the way he challenges you. He's a good, good player and a player to look out for in the future."

England have been waiting to face an opponent who will match their Premier League style of play.

Norway had 66 per cent of the ball in their 2-1 last-16 victory over Brazil - and Bodo/Glimt's possession-based style influence in the team is clear to see.

Bjortuft added: "Norwegian football is getting really good possession-wise. We have players who can really control the game and use the ball.

"I think we saw it against Brazil. More than 60 per cent possession against a really strong ball-playing team.

"It shows how we play. At the same time, I think if England give Norway room and space, there's no doubt we have a counter-attacking team as well, with, of course, Haaland at the front, but also really good wingers who can challenge players one-on-one.

"I think our football is more possession-based, but if we can attack sharp and smooth, we'll do it."
